notes:
I have gathered material from Enduring Word, Precept Austin, Gill, Ellicott, Haydock (Catholic), Barnes, Keil & Delitzsch, and others. Here are the verse-by-verse notes:

---

## Joshua 2 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### v. 1a — Joshua sends two spies secretly from Shittim

**Traditional Reading:**

Joshua’s sending of spies was evidence of faithful preparation, not unbelief. God had promised success (Josh. 1:3–6), but the promises were meant to encourage faith-filled activity, not passivity (Guzik, Enduring Word). Keil & Delitzsch note that “although Joshua had received a promise from the Lord of His almighty help…he still thought it necessary to do what was requisite on his part to secure the success of the work committed to him, as the help of God does not preclude human action, but rather presupposes it” (Precept Austin, citing Keil & Delitzsch). Gill adds that the Hebrew word translated “secretly” (*cheresh*) means “silently”—the secrecy was likely to prevent another disastrous public report like that of the ten spies in Numbers 13 (Guzik; Gill notes Jewish speculations that the two were Caleb and Phinehas but says this is improbable).

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-2/
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-2-commentary
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/joshua/2.htm

**Baptist View:** The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary emphasises Joshua “taking the initiative in preparing for conquest of Canaan, though the Lord has yet given him no specific instructions.” The information gained “would serve to encourage and embolden Israel” (Garner-Howes, StudyLight).

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/joshua-2.html

**Orthodox/Catholic:** Haydock notes Joshua’s prudence: he sent only two men rather than twelve to avoid the earlier failure, and “secretly” so as not to alarm the Israelites (Haydock, biblehub.com).

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/joshua/2.htm

---

### v. 1b — The spies enter the house of Rahab the harlot

**Traditional Reading:**

The description of Rahab as a “harlot” (Hebrew *zanah*, LXX *porne*) has embarrassed some interpreters who tried to call her an “innkeeper,” but Hebrews 11:31 and James 2:25 confirm she was a prostitute (Guzik; Precept Austin; Gill). Calvin called the “innkeeper” interpretation a “presumptuous wresting of Scripture” (Pulpit Commentary excerpt in search results). Gill notes the Jewish Targum of Jonathan calls her an “innkeeper or victualler,” but he and most commentators reject this. The harlot’s house was a good place for anonymous strangers to avoid detection (Guzik; Precept Austin). Guzik cites Hess: “The text carefully avoids implying a sexual liaison between the spies and their hostess.” Grant (cited by Precept Austin) notes the language of “lodged” (*sakab*) is used for sleeping, not sexual relations—sexual use of the verb requires the preposition “with.”

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-2/
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-2-commentary
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/joshua/2.htm

**Baptist View:** The Garner-Howes commentary states: “The Lord had guided them to the house of Rahab the harlot, who had already been convicted of the truth concerning these invading people. In this is seen the overruling hand of God with His people” (Garner-Howes, StudyLight).

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/joshua-2.html

**Catholic View:** Haydock comments that “innkeeper” was sometimes the interpretation of the Hebrew and Chaldee, but that Rahab’s being a harlot is the plainer sense, and that she became a convert. The genealogy of Christ (Mt 1:5) includes her without shame, showing God’s grace.

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/joshua/2.htm

**Older Commentators:** Origen (3rd homily on Joshua, cited by Pulpit and Guzik) saw a typology: “As the first Jesus sent his spies before him and they were received into the harlot’s house, so the second Jesus sent His forerunners, whom the publicans and harlots gladly received.”

---

### vv. 2–3 — The king of Jericho learns of the spies and demands their surrender

**Traditional Reading:**

The king’s intelligence network detected the Israelite men. The city was already on high alert due to fear of the approaching Israelites (Guzik). Gill notes the king may have employed watchers, or citizens reported the strangers out of self-preservation. The king sent directly to Rahab, indicating informants had tracked the spies to her house.

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-2/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/joshua/2.htm

**Precept Austin** adds: “Somehow, the leader of the city-state of Jericho learned that two Israelite men had come to the city as spies.”

— https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-2-commentary

---

### vv. 4–5 — Rahab hides the spies and deceives the king’s men

**Traditional Reading:**

Rahab “had taken the two men and hid them” before the messengers arrived. Her lie — “I did not know where they were from” and “the men went out… I do not know which way they went” — is reported by Scripture without explicit praise or condemnation. Guzik says: “The Bible simply reports Rahab’s lie; it does not praise it or excuse it. Rahab faced an ethical challenge: either option was bad. She decided that it was worse for her to betray the spies than to lie about their presence.” Ellicott says the falsehood “evidently left no stain on Rahab’s conscience, although all falsehood is sin,” noting that “the Divine standard of sin and holiness never varies; but the standard of man’s conscience, even when faith is a dominant principle in the character, may vary to a very considerable degree.”

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-2/
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-2.html

Gill observes: “She might not scruple telling a lie, being brought up a Heathen…though her lies are not to be justified; evil is not to be done that good may come; nor are men to tell lies one to another upon any account; but these sins, with others, the Lord forgave her.”

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/joshua/2.htm

**Baptist View:** “Rahab cannot be exonerated for her falsehood concerning the men, but her action may be explained due to her pagan background and immaturity in the Lord. The Lord’s will was accomplished, nevertheless, although He would doubtless have protected them had she told the truth about them” (Garner-Howes).

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/joshua-2.html

**Reformed/Evangelical:** Trapp (cited by Guzik) says: “This was an act of her praiseworthy faith. See Hebrews 11:31, where it is honourably mentioned, but nothing is said of the lie she told. God layeth the finger of mercy on the scars of our sins.”

---

### v. 6 — Rahab had hidden the spies on the roof under stalks of flax

**Traditional Reading:**

Flat roofs were common in the ancient Near East and were used for drying crops. Gill notes that flax was bound in bundles and dried in the sun before being stripped and beaten. Ellicott observes that “flax and barley are both early crops (Exodus 9:31), and that the first month (see Joshua 4:19) was the time of barley harvest,” fitting the spring timeframe. The stalks provided convenient cover for the men.

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-2.html
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/joshua/2.htm

---

### v. 7 — The pursuers head toward the Jordan fords; the gate is shut

**Traditional Reading:**

The king’s men took Rahab’s misdirection and pursued toward the Jordan fords, the logical crossing point back to the Israelite camp. As soon as the pursuers left, the city gate was shut — sealing the spies inside but also preventing the pursuers from easily returning (Gill). This detail shows the thoroughness of the city’s defences and the providential timing protecting the spies.

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/joshua/2.htm

---

### vv. 8–11 — Rahab’s confession of faith

**Traditional Reading:**

Rahab’s confession is the theological heart of the chapter. Ellicott calls her words “memorable in every way” and notes the fulfilment of the song of Moses (Exodus 15:15–16): “All the inhabitants of Canaan shall melt away.” Her confession — “the LORD your God, He is God in heaven above and on earth beneath” — is language used in Israel’s own creedal confessions (Ex. 20:4; Deut. 4:39; 5:8) (Guzik). Guzik notes: “This surprising outburst of faith shows that God had a plan in bringing Rahab and the spies together. God had already been speaking to Rahab in some way.” She had heard of the Red Sea crossing and the defeat of Sihon and Og — events that were forty years old and events just months old, respectively.

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-2/
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-2.html

Gill remarks: “This is a proof of her knowledge of the true God, and faith in Him, and shows her to be a believer, and hence she is reckoned in the catalogue of believers, Hebrews 11:31.”

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/joshua/2.htm

**Precept Austin** emphasises the contrast: “Of all the Canaanite people at the time of Israel’s conquest of the land, Rahab is the only one known to have genuinely converted to Israel’s God.” Her faith was informed by what she had heard — likely from travellers visiting her establishment (Boice, cited by Guzik).

— https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-2-commentary

**Ellicott** compares her confession favourably even with Israel’s own faith: “Did the faith of the men of Israel go much further than this? Did it always go so far? (Comp. Joshua 24:14; 1 Kings 18:21; Jonah 1:9–10). The prophets themselves could not assert much more.”

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-2.html

---

### vv. 12–13 — Rahab’s plea: an oath, kindness for her family, and a “sure sign”

**Traditional Reading:**

Rahab asks the spies to “swear…by the LORD” — she invokes the name of Yahweh, showing her faith. She asks for *hesed* (“kindness”) for her “father’s house” — father, mother, brothers, sisters, and all belonging to them. Ellicott notes: “Whatever Rahab may have been herself, her acknowledgment of all her family is observable. She was in no way separated or degraded from their society.” Gill observes she “makes no mention of any husband or children she had, as harlots seldom have,” which seems to confirm her former life.

Guzik adds: “Rahab’s desire to see her family saved, and the effort she made to save their lives, shows that her love should be noticed, as well as her faith.”

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-2/
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-2.html
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/joshua/2.htm

**Catholic View (Haydock):** She demands a “true token” — “such a one as, when I shew it to the Israelites, they may preserve me and mine. She is not content with a verbal promise, she requires something permanent and sensible, as a mark of their mutual engagements” (Haydock, biblehub.com).

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/joshua/2.htm

---

### v. 14 — The spies pledge their lives: “Our lives for your lives”

**Traditional Reading:**

The spies make a solemn oath: “Our lives for yours” — literally “our souls in your stead to die” (Gill). The condition is “if you do not report our mission” — i.e., she must keep their secret. They promise “kindness and faithfulness” (Hebrew *hesed ve’emet*) when the LORD gives them the land. Guzik notes: “Joshua is a book of harsh judgment on the Canaanites, but the first story dealing with someone other than Joshua is about God’s mercy to an unlikely yet believing Canaanite.”

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-2/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/joshua/2.htm

---

### vv. 15–16 — Rahab lets them down by a rope; she directs them to the hill country

**Traditional Reading:**

Rahab’s house was built into the city wall, giving direct access to the outside. This was strategically perfect for escape. Ellicott comments: “Happily for the two spies. Perhaps, indeed, they selected it for this reason, as it enabled them to leave the town without passing the gate.” She tells them to hide in “the hill country” (likely the limestone hills west of Jericho, known as Jebel Karantu or Quarantania — JFB) for three days until pursuers give up (Gill; Ellicott).

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-2.html
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/joshua/2.htm

**Jamieson-Fausset-Brown** note: “A range of white limestone hills extends on the north…rising to a height of from twelve hundred to fifteen hundred feet, and the sides of which are perforated with caves. Some one peak adjoining was familiarly known to the inhabitants as ‘the mountain.’”

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/joshua/2.htm

---

### vv. 17–20 — The scarlet cord and the conditions of safety

**Traditional Reading:**

The spies clarify the conditions: Rahab must (1) tie the “scarlet cord” (*tikvath hashani*) in the window through which they escaped, and (2) gather all her family into her house. Anyone leaving the house forfeits protection — “his blood will be on his own head.” If she betrays their mission, the oath is void.

Ellicott makes an important distinction: “The scarlet line and the cord by which the men were lowered are not the same thing, but described by different words in the original. It would have been preposterous to require Rahab to display in her window the means by which the spies had escaped…it would at once have declared the tale to all beholders.” Rather, the “line of scarlet thread” was a separate item — a visible but unsuspicious marker.

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-2.html

Keil & Delitzsch, however, argue that “this cord” refers back to the rope of v. 15: “The demonstrative ‘this’ leads to the conclusion adopted by Luther and others, that ‘this cord’ is the rope mentioned in Joshua 2:15.” They see the crimson colour as “the colour of vigorous life, [making] this cord an expressive sign of the preservation of Rahab’s life.”

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/kad/joshua/2.htm

**Typology of the Scarlet Cord:** From Clement of Rome (1st century) onward, the Church Fathers saw the scarlet cord as a type of Christ’s blood. Barnes notes: “The use of scarlet in the Levitical rites…naturally led the fathers, from Clement of Rome onward, to see in this scarlet thread, no less than in the blood of the Passover, an emblem of salvation by the Blood of Christ.” Guzik adds that Justin Martyr, Irenaeus, and Origen all held this view. Spurgeon (cited by Guzik) said: “Rahab tied the scarlet line, not in some secret part of the house, but in the window. It was her public declaration of faith.”

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-2/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/joshua/2.htm

**Ellicott** also draws the Passover parallel: “What the blood was to the houses of Israel in Egypt, that the scarlet line in the window was to the house of Rahab. Both alike prefigured ‘the precious blood of Christ’” (citing Exodus 12:22).

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-2.html

**Catholic View (Haydock):** “If she had instructed others of her fellow-citizens to hand out the same mark, she would have forfeited all her privileges” — emphasising the exclusivity of the sign and her duty of secrecy.

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/joshua/2.htm

---

### v. 21 — “Let it be as you say”; Rahab ties the scarlet cord

**Traditional Reading:**

Rahab’s response is immediate obedience: “According to your words, so be it.” She sent the men away and “tied the scarlet cord in the window.” Guzik notes: “Though known only to Rahab and the Israelites, this was a declaration of her allegiance with Israel and the God of Israel.” Keil & Delitzsch clarify that “it is not to be supposed that she did this at once, but merely as soon as it was necessary. It is mentioned here for the purpose of bringing the subject to a close” — since the conquest was still days away.

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-2/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/kad/joshua/2.htm

**Baptist View (Spurgeon):** Spurgeon preached an entire sermon on Rahab’s faith, calling it “saving faith, singular faith, stable faith, self-denying faith, sympathising faith, and sanctifying faith.” Of the scarlet cord, he said: “Let it be a scarlet line that you tie in the window…namely, an avowal of true faith in his precious blood, a declaration of confidence in atonement by blood; for there are some who profess a sort of faith, but it is not faith in the substitution of Christ.”

— https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/rahabs-faith

---

### vv. 22–24 — The spies hide three days and return with a faith-filled report

**Traditional Reading:**

The spies obeyed Rahab’s instruction, hiding in the hill country three days. The pursuers searched “all along the road” but found nothing. The spies returned to Joshua and reported: “The LORD has surely delivered the entire land into our hands…all who dwell in the land are melting in fear of us.”

Guzik observes that the spies’ report contained nothing essential for the military conquest of Jericho — the battle strategy would come from God alone, not human intelligence. The greater purpose of the mission “was to arrange and assure the salvation of Rahab and her family.” Ellicott says simply: “Observe the entirely satisfactory effect of this mission.”

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-2/
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-2.html

**Precept Austin** notes the parallel with Gideon (Judges 7:13–15): “What Gideon heard gave encouragement through the words of an enemy…From the mouth of somebody on ‘the other side’ came a verbalization that completely settled the situation” (citing Schaeffer).

— https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-2-commentary

**Baptist View:** The Garner-Howes commentary concludes: “From the things of Joshua 2, let us learn 1) the Lord allows us to prove Him and learn for ourselves that He can make us overcome in all situations; 2) the mighty deeds of the Lord on behalf of His people ought to convict the world today of His greatness; 3) comparatively, there are still very few who respond and turn to the Lord from the world; 4) once convicted of the Lord’s leadership and will in us we may then encourage others by our own willingness to trust Him.”

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/joshua-2.html

---

## Summary of Tradition-Specific Differences

**On Rahab’s Lie (vv. 4–5):**

- **Gill (Baptist/Reformed):** The lie is not justified; “evil is not to be done that good may come”; the Lord forgave her.
- **Ellicott (Anglican):** The falsehood “left no stain on Rahab’s conscience” because her conscience was not yet fully formed by God’s law; the divine standard never varies but human conscience does.
- **Garner-Howes (Baptist):** “Rahab cannot be exonerated for her falsehood…but her action may be explained due to her pagan background and immaturity in the Lord.”
- **Trapp (Puritan/Reformed):** God “layeth the finger of mercy on the scars of our sins” — Hebrews 11 mentions her faith, not her lie.

**On the Scarlet Cord (v. 18):**

- **Ellicott, Barnes, Guzik (broad Evangelical):** The scarlet cord typologically prefigures the blood of Christ, following Clement of Rome, Justin Martyr, Irenaeus, Origen, and Spurgeon.
- **Keil & Delitzsch (Lutheran/Conservative):** The crimson colour symbolises “vigorous life” and preservation; they identify the “cord” as the same rope used for the escape.
- **Ellicott:** The scarlet line and the escape rope are *different items* in the Hebrew; displaying the escape rope would have been absurd and would have betrayed the secret.
- **Haydock (Catholic):** Emphasises the exclusivity — if Rahab had shared the sign with others, she would have forfeited protection.

**On Rahab’s Profession (v. 1):**

- **Calvin (Reformed):** Rejected “innkeeper” as a “presumptuous wresting of Scripture.”
- **Jewish Targum and some rabbis:** Called her an “innkeeper” (*pundeqita*) to soften the scandal.
- **All Protestant traditions surveyed:** Affirm she was a harlot, while noting the text avoids implying any sexual misconduct by the spies.
- **Catholic (Haydock):** Acknowledges the “innkeeper” possibility from the Hebrew/Chaldee but accepts “harlot” as the plain sense, seeing her conversion as evidence of grace.

**On Faith and Works (James 2:25 connection):**

- **Precept Austin (Evangelical/Dispensational):** Rahab was “shown to be justified” — her works proved her faith was genuine. The root of faith was demonstrated by the fruit of works.
- **Spurgeon (Baptist):** Her faith was “saving faith…singular faith…self-denying faith” — she risked her life, showing faith and works together.
- This is broadly agreed across traditions — all cite Hebrews 11:31 and James 2:25.
